questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] noisy neighbours and per-tenant fairness on one shared stack (grok-build-multitenant, dfableandopus/05-SYSTEM-DESIGN-FOLLOWUPS.md). Scenario: one tenant's integration now sends about 900 of the app's 1,400 requests a second and every tenant's p99 latency rises with it; four API instances share one PostgreSQL. The review this triggered also found last week's near-miss: a per-instance response cache, added to the project list to soak up that load, was keyed without the organization and for a few minutes served one tenant's project list to another. Write your design before you look: what a rate limit is keyed on and where in the request path it runs, how database connections are shared (or reserved) between tenants, how you learn which tenant is spending what, how every cache key carries the tenant and how you find the cache that does not, and what the heavy tenant receives when it reaches its budget. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] The budget belongs to the organization, because the organization is what pays and what can multiply its callers: one customer can own many users and service accounts. The only trustworthy organization id is the one the tenant middleware attaches after it has found a membership row for the verified user, so the per-tenant bucket is keyed on that value.

[w3] Placement is a security decision: the organization header is only a selection, so a bucket keyed on the raw header before membership is checked lets anyone drain a victim tenant's budget by naming its id. Run a cheap per-caller guard first and the per-organization bucket after the membership check, accepting that each refused request has already cost one membership query.
[w2] The bucket lives in shared state: the one limiter the code has today is per-process memory, and with four instances each would hand the heavy tenant a full budget of its own.
keyPoints.quote: The login limiter is a `Map` created inside `authRoutes`

keyPoints.text: [w3] Connections are the resource the heavy tenant actually takes: each process builds one global database client, with no pool settings of its own, and every tenant's requests draw from that one pool alike. Cap in-flight requests per organization per instance so no single tenant can hold the whole pool.

[w3] The cache leak has a structural cause: the tenant is not in the URL. The client sends the bearer token and the selected organization as headers, so the list URL is the same string for every tenant and a cache keyed on it mixes them. Build every key through one function that demands the verified tenant context, so a key without the organization cannot be constructed.

[w2] Today every API response is marked no-store, which is what keeps browsers and intermediaries from holding tenant data; keep that header, and treat any shared HTTP cache placed in front of the API as a new tenant boundary that needs its own keying review.

[w2] Nobody can name the expensive tenant today: only responses of 500 and above are logged, carrying a request id and a status, with no organization, route or duration. Record organization, route, duration and database time per request and rank tenants by spend before choosing their limits.

[w1] An over-budget tenant gets a 429 with a Retry-After the integration can obey (the shape the sign-in throttle already uses), plus a visible quota, so its client backs off instead of retrying into the queue.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — fairness rollout week on the same design: the first limiter that ships is keyed on user id, and the heavy tenant's integration runs as 40 service accounts; the same tenant starts a full export whose transactions hold connections for minutes, and the load balancer begins removing instances whose health checks time out; and the cache fix ships, but a second response cache, added at the HTTP layer in front of the project list, still keys on the URL. What breaks first, how does it show, and what is the repair?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Forty service accounts each get a full per-user budget, so the limiter admits forty times what was meant for the tenant and the neighbours see no relief. The verified tenant context already holds both ids; key the main bucket on the organization and keep the per-user bucket only as a sub-limit inside it.

[w3] Healthy instances are pulled because the health route runs its probe query through the same pool as tenant traffic: once the export's long transactions hold every connection, the probe waits in line like any request and times out, and one tenant's job becomes an outage for all. Give the probe a path that does not queue behind tenant work, and cap how many connections one tenant may hold.

[w3] The second cache leaks for the same reason as the first: tenant and identity travel in headers, so a URL-keyed HTTP cache sees one list for everyone. Fixing one layer fixes only that layer; audit every cache for its key, vary or bypass on the tenant headers, and keep a test where two tenants request the same URL and must receive disjoint bodies.

[w2] The export holds connections because it reads like the list endpoint: a repeatable-read transaction that pages and counts keeps its connection for the whole snapshot. Export in short, separately committed pages so each one gives its connection back.
[w2] The first signal is everyone's p99 because nothing records the tenant per request; attaching the organization to each log line is what turns a global latency alarm into the name of one customer.
keyPoints.quote: Third, tag every log line with the organization id from `req.tenant`

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your fairness design against the alternatives: per-tenant versus per-user limits, one shared connection pool with per-tenant caps versus connections reserved per plan tier, the organization id in every cache key versus a separate cache per tenant versus not caching tenant data at all, rejecting over-budget requests versus queueing them, and a limiter in process memory versus one in a shared store. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A per-tenant limit matches who pays and cannot be multiplied by adding accounts, but one runaway user inside a tenant can starve their own colleagues; per-user limits alone are fair inside a tenant and useless against a tenant with many accounts. The tenant context carries both ids, so a per-user cap nested inside the tenant budget costs little.

[w3] Reserving connections per plan tier guarantees paying tiers their capacity but leaves reserved connections idle, and the organization record has no plan or tier at all, so it starts with a schema change and a pool per tier; one shared pool with per-tenant caps uses every connection and guarantees nothing to anyone under pressure.

[w3] The organization in every key keeps one cache and one eviction budget but rests on every key builder remembering it; a cache per tenant makes a cross-tenant hit structurally impossible and fragments memory across thousands of tenants; not caching tenant data is today's posture, where the membership is re-read on every request, and its cost is database load that grows with traffic.
keyPoints.quote: which is the first thing anyone will want to cache

keyPoints.text: [w2] Rejecting with 429 keeps latency predictable for everyone else and moves backoff to the integration; queueing smooths bursts but holds memory and, worse, connections or request slots for each waiting call, which are exactly what the limit protects.

[w2] A limiter in process memory costs nothing per request but multiplies its budget by the instance count and forgets everything on restart; a shared store gives one true budget at the cost of a network hop per request and a dependency whose outage needs a written fail-open or fail-closed choice.
